etymology: Hebrew Shaphir, “fair” or “beautiful,” a town of the Judean lowland named in Micah’s lament, whose lovely name is turned against it in judgment.
biblical_def: Saphir means “fair,” and Micah makes its beauty the very edge of his sorrow. Marching in prophecy through the doomed towns of the Shephelah, he cries: “Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked” (Mic 1:11). The town whose name is Beautiful is stripped and led away in shameful captivity, its loveliness no defence against the wrath of God. Micah, “the Morasthite” who prophesied “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Mic 1:1), saw the Assyrian storm break upon Judah’s own doorstep: “her wound is incurable; for it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem” (Mic 1:9). The prophet bids the land mourn: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children…for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). Saphir preaches that outward beauty is no shield against sin’s wages. The fair town is stripped bare; the comely city is carried captive; what men admire, God judges if it be found in rebellion. Beauty is a gift, not a covering; only righteousness clothes the soul against the day of wrath. The inhabitant of Saphir walks away naked, and her name mocks her ruin until it teaches the lesson: loveliness without holiness cannot stand.
webster_summary: A lowland town of Judah in Micah’s lament (Mic 1:11) whose name means “fair”; stripped and led captive, a witness that beauty is no shield against the wages of sin.

corruption_paragraphs: Saphir rebukes the ancient confusion that mistakes beauty for safety and admiration for approval. The town named Fair is led away naked and ashamed, its comeliness powerless against the judgment its sin had earned. Micah turns the lovely name into an instrument of grief, that the lesson might strike home.

The modern form of this corruption exalts the beautiful and the admired as though loveliness were its own justification — the cult of image, appearance, and the pleasing surface. But Saphir teaches that God judges the heart, not the face, and that beauty found in rebellion is stripped bare in the day of reckoning. Only the righteousness of Christ clothes the soul; every other covering is torn away. Let the fair take warning and the comely take heed: what men praise, God weighs, and beauty without holiness cannot stand before Him.

etymology: Hebrew Tsa'anan, likely “going out” or “place of flocks,” a town of the Judean lowland named in Micah’s lament in a pun upon its name.
biblical_def: Zaanan means “going out,” and Micah makes a bitter wordplay of it: the town whose name is Sally-forth cannot sally forth. “The inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth in the mourning of Bethezel” (Mic 1:11). When judgment falls, the people who should march out to battle or flee to safety are paralysed, shut up within their walls, unable to move. The prophet Micah “saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Mic 1:1) a doom that had come home to Judah: “it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem” (Mic 1:9). And over the whole ravaged land he raised the cry, “evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem” (Mic 1:12). Zaanan preaches the helplessness of the sinner under the hand of God. The town that lived by going out is frozen where it stands; the strength that men presume upon fails them utterly in the hour of wrath. There is a paralysis that falls upon the guilty when God arises to judge, so that they can neither fight nor flee. Only He who binds can loose; and the sinner who would go out from the prison of his guilt must wait upon the mercy of God, for no strength of his own will open the gate.

corruption_paragraphs: Zaanan rebukes the presumption of self-sufficiency. The town named for going out is frozen where it stands when God arises; the strength men trust in fails them utterly in the hour of wrath. The wordplay is a warning: what you boast of will betray you when the LORD lays His hand upon you.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the total helplessness of the sinner apart from grace. The age preaches human capacity, resilience, and the power to break every chain by will; but Zaanan cannot come forth. There is a bondage of guilt that no native strength can loose, a paralysis that falls upon the guilty when God judges. Only He who binds can free. The sinner who would go out from the prison-house of his sin must wait upon the mercy of God in Christ, who alone opens the gate and proclaims liberty to the captive.

etymology: Hebrew Maroth, “bitterness” (kin to Marah), a town of the Judean lowland named in Micah’s lament, whose hope for good was answered with evil.
biblical_def: Maroth means “bitterness,” and its portion matched its name. “For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem” (Mic 1:12). The town watched anxiously for deliverance, straining for some turn of mercy, but what came down was judgment, and it came from the LORD Himself, reaching even to the gate of Jerusalem. Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of the kings of Judah “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Mic 1:1), and declared the wound incurable: “it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people” (Mic 1:9). The land is bidden to mourn its captive children: “for they are gone into captivity from thee” (Mic 1:16). Maroth preaches two solemn truths. First, that evil, in the sense of calamity and judgment, comes down from the LORD; He is sovereign over the rod as over the blessing, and the sinner who presumes upon a mercy he has not sought waits in vain. Second, that a hope which is not grounded in repentance is only bitterness deferred. Maroth watched for good while clinging to its sin, and reaped the bitterness of its name. True hope waits upon God in penitence, not in presumption; else the watching ends in wormwood.

corruption_paragraphs: Maroth rebukes the presumptuous hope that waits for good while clinging to sin. The town strained for deliverance, but evil came down from the LORD, for it had not turned from the rebellion that earned the rod. Its bitter name became its bitter portion, hope deferred souring into wormwood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: that calamity itself comes down from the sovereign hand of God (Amos 3:6), and that hope severed from repentance is only bitterness postponed. The modern spirit expects good as its due, apart from any turning to God, and calls the expectation optimism. But Maroth watched for good with an unhumbled heart and reaped the evil it would not repent of. True hope waits upon the LORD in penitence and faith, resting on His mercy in Christ; every other watching ends where Maroth’s did, in the bitterness its name foretold.

etymology: Hebrew Moresheth Gath, “possession of Gath,” a town of the Judean lowland, the home of the prophet Micah, distinct from the Philistine Gath.
biblical_def: Moresheth-gath was Micah’s own home, for he is called “the Morasthite” (Mic 1:1) — the man of Moresheth. In his lament over the doomed towns of the lowland, the prophet does not spare the region of his birth: “Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moreshethgath: the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel” (Mic 1:14). The image is of a father giving a parting dowry to a daughter passing away to another house — Judah must send Moresheth-gath off like a bride departing, surrendered to the conqueror. Micah, who “saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Mic 1:1), declared that the blow had reached Judah’s gate: “he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem” (Mic 1:9), and bade the land mourn its captive children (Mic 1:16). Moresheth-gath preaches that the true prophet spares not even his own. Micah wept for his homeland yet spoke its doom plainly, loving his people too well to flatter them. The faithful watchman does not exempt his own house, his own town, his own kindred, from the word of God. Nathan of the manse and Amos of the herds and Micah of Moresheth all learned that the word entrusted to them must fall where God aims it, even upon the fields where they were born.

corruption_paragraphs: Moresheth-gath rebukes the partiality that would soften God’s word where it touches our own. Micah loved his native lowland, yet he pronounced its doom without flinching, giving it up like a father surrendering a daughter to a far country. He wept, but he did not flatter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impartial faithfulness of the true prophet, who spares neither his own town nor his own kindred when God aims the word there. The temptation of every minister is to preach hardest against sins that are far off and to fall silent where the word would wound his own. But Micah of Moresheth, Amos of Tekoa, and Nathan before David all learned that the message belongs to God, not to the messenger’s comfort. Love for one’s people is proved, not by flattery, but by faithfulness that tells them the truth even to their loss.

etymology: Hebrew Beth le-'Aphrah, “house of dust,” a town of the Judean lowland named in Micah’s lament, where the prophet bids the people roll in the dust of mourning.
biblical_def: Beth-le-aphrah means “house of dust,” and Micah seizes the name to summon the town to the very act of mourning it signifies: “in the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust” (Mic 1:10). The same verse warns against telling the shameful news to the enemy: “Declare ye it not at Gath, weep ye not at all,” echoing David’s lament over Saul lest the Philistines rejoice. Micah the Morasthite, who prophesied “concerning Samaria and Jerusalem” (Mic 1:1), saw the wound reach Judah’s gate: “it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people” (Mic 1:9), and called the land to sackcloth for its captive children (Mic 1:16). Beth-le-aphrah preaches the fitness of humiliation before God. The house of dust is called to remember that it is dust, to sink low in penitence under the mighty hand of God. Dust is the sign of mortality and of mourning; Abraham confessed himself dust and ashes, and Job repented in dust. The sinner under judgment is bidden to take his true place, rolling in the dust of a broken and contrite heart. Such lowliness is not despair but the doorway of mercy, for the LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, and He raises the humble from the dust to set them among princes.

corruption_paragraphs: Beth-le-aphrah rebukes the pride that will not stoop. The house of dust is called to remember that it is dust and to sink low in penitence; but the natural heart resents the summons, counting humiliation beneath its dignity. Micah bids the town do what its name declares: roll in the dust before the God it has offended.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the necessity and blessedness of humiliation before God. The modern spirit prizes self-esteem and recoils from repentance as demeaning; but the way up is down. Abraham confessed himself dust and ashes, Job repented in dust, and the publican who smote his breast went down justified. To roll in the dust of a broken and contrite heart is not despair but the doorway of mercy, for the LORD is nigh the broken-hearted and lifts the humble from the dust to set them among princes.

etymology: Hebrew Tob, “good,” a region east of Gilead where the outcast Jephthah found refuge before God raised him to deliver Israel.
biblical_def: The land of Tob was the place of an exile’s refuge and the making of a deliverer. Jephthah the Gileadite, though “a mighty man of valour” (Jdg 11:1), was cast out by his brethren as the son of a harlot, and he fled: “Then Jephthah fled from his brethren, and dwelt in the land of Tob” (Jdg 11:3), where vain men gathered to him. But when the Ammonites made war, the elders of Gilead who had rejected him came seeking the very man they despised: “the elders of Gilead went to fetch Jephthah out of the land of Tob” (Jdg 11:5). The region was known in the wars of the east; its men were hired against David: “and of king Maacah a thousand men, and of Ishtob twelve thousand men” (2Sa 10:6). Tob, whose name means “good,” preaches the good providence of God toward the rejected. The stone the builders refused God made the head of the corner. Jephthah, disinherited and driven out, was hidden in Tob until the LORD’s hour, then called back to save the brethren who had cast him off. Here is a shadow of a greater Rejected One, despised and refused by His own, who became the Deliverer of the very people that would not have Him. God prepares His chosen instruments in obscurity and exile, and brings them forth in His time.

corruption_paragraphs: Tob faces no modern quarrel, but Jephthah’s refuge there rebukes the worldly reckoning that writes off the rejected and the lowborn. His brethren despised him as the son of a harlot and drove him out; God hid him in the land named Good and made him the deliverer of the very men who cast him away.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the good providence of God toward the despised and the exiled. The stone the builders refused becomes the head of the corner. God prepares His instruments in obscurity — Moses in Midian, David among the sheep, Jephthah in Tob — and brings them forth in His hour. Above all, Tob foreshadows the great Rejected One, despised and refused by His own, who became the Saviour of the people that would not have Him. Let the outcast take heart: the land of exile may be the very place where God is making a deliverer.

etymology: Hebrew Mitspah, “watchtower” or “beacon,” a place east of Jordan in Gilead, the site of Jacob’s covenant with Laban and of Jephthah’s vow, distinct from Mizpah in Benjamin.
biblical_def: Mizpah of Gilead means “watchtower,” and it was named for the watch that God keeps between men. There Jacob and Laban raised their heap of witness and parted, and Laban said: “And Mizpah; for he said, The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another” (Gen 31:49). It is the origin of the “Mizpah” blessing, though spoken first not in sweet fellowship but as a wary covenant between two men who did not trust each other — a plea that God would be the witness and judge of both. Long after, this Mizpah of Gilead became the mustering-place of Israel against Ammon and the scene of Jephthah’s tragic vow: “the children of Israel…encamped in Mizpeh” (Jdg 10:17); “Jephthah uttered all his words before the LORD in Mizpeh” (Jdg 11:11); and thence “he passed over Mizpeh of Gilead…unto the children of Ammon” (Jdg 11:29). Mizpah preaches that God watches between man and man. He is the unseen witness of every covenant, promise, and parting; He marks the dealings of the absent and will judge the false and vindicate the true. The Mizpah word is no mere sentiment of farewell but a solemn invocation: the LORD watch between us, for He sees what men hide, and to Him both parties must answer. Where men cannot trust each other, the fear of the watching God must hold them.

corruption_paragraphs: Mizpah is often reduced to a sentimental farewell, a warm wish between friends who part. But its original was a wary covenant between Jacob and Laban, two men who did not trust each other and invoked God as watchman and judge lest either deal falsely with the other. The word is a solemn oath, not a greeting-card blessing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God watches between man and man, the unseen witness of every covenant, promise, and parting. He sees what men conceal in absence and will judge the false and vindicate the true. This truth restrains the deceitful and comforts the wronged: where men cannot trust each other, the fear of the watching God must hold them. Rightly understood, the Mizpah word calls both parties to answer to the LORD, who keeps the account no human eye can see, and who will one day set every hidden dealing in the light.

etymology: Hebrew Netophah, “a dropping” or “distillation,” a village near Bethlehem, home of returning exiles and of two of David’s mighty men.
biblical_def: Netophah was a small village near Bethlehem, and its glory lies in the faithfulness of its obscure sons. Its men returned from the Babylonian captivity to rebuild the ruined land: “The men of Netophah, fifty and six” (Ezr 2:22), reckoned again with Bethlehem in Nehemiah’s roll: “The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, an hundred fourscore and eight” (Neh 7:26). The village belonged to the sons of Salma with Bethlehem: “The sons of Salma; Bethlehem, and the Netophathites” (1Ch 2:54). And from Netophah came valiant men in David’s guard: “Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai the Netophathite” (2Sa 23:28). A hamlet of no renown gave loyal soldiers to the king and faithful pilgrims to the return. Netophah preaches the honour God sets upon the faithful obscure. The men of a nameless village are written in the sacred rolls beside the great, numbered among the returning remnant and the mighty men of David. The kingdom of God is built not chiefly by the celebrated but by the multitude of the faithful unknown — the fifty-six who came home to rebuild, the plain soldier who stood by his king. etymology: Hebrew Beth hak-Kerem, “house of the vineyard,” a town of Judah near Jerusalem used as a beacon-station for the fire-signal of alarm.
biblical_def: Beth-haccerem means “house of the vineyard,” and it stood upon a height where the watchmen kindled the signal-fire of war. Jeremiah names it as the beacon of alarm when the northern foe advanced: “blow the trumpet in Tekoa, and set up a sign of fire in Bethhaccerem: for evil appeareth out of the north, and great destruction” (Jer 6:1). In the days of rebuilding, its ruler shared in the repair of the walls: “the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem” (Neh 3:14). The name joins two images that run through Scripture — the vineyard and the watch. Israel itself is the LORD’s vineyard: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa 5:7), the vine He planted and tended, singing over it, “My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill” (Isa 5:1). Yet the house of the vineyard became a tower of alarm, for the vine that yielded wild grapes must be warned of the coming rod. Beth-haccerem preaches the double office of the church: to be God’s cultivated vineyard and His watchtower of warning. Where the vine grows fruitful, the beacon rests; where it turns wild, the fire is kindled and the trumpet blown. The faithful watchman on the vineyard-height cries the alarm of judgment, that the people may turn before the destruction out of the north.

corruption_paragraphs: Beth-haccerem joins the vineyard and the watch, and its lesson rebukes a church that would keep the comfort of the vineyard while silencing the alarm of the watchtower. Israel was the LORD’s planted vine, yet when it yielded wild grapes the beacon-fire of Beth-haccerem had to be kindled and the trumpet blown.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the church’s double office: to be God’s cultivated vineyard and His watchtower of warning. The age loves the vineyard’s wine but hates the watchman’s trumpet, preferring a religion of comfort with no cry of judgment. But love that will not warn is not love. The faithful watchman on the vineyard-height sounds the alarm of the coming rod, that the people may turn before the destruction out of the north. To keep silent when the sword approaches is to let the blood of the perishing be required at the watchman’s hand (Eze 33:6).

etymology: Greek Harimathaia, a town of the Jews (likely the Ramah of the Old Testament), the home of Joseph who buried the body of Jesus.
biblical_def: Arimathaea is remembered for one man and one deed. “When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathaea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus’ disciple” (Mat 27:57). All four Gospels honour him at the cross’s aftermath. He was “an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God” and “went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus” (Mar 15:43). He had stood apart from the guilt of the council: “he was of Arimathaea, a city of the Jews: who also himself waited for the kingdom of God” (Luk 23:51). And though once timid, in the hour of danger he found courage: “Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews” (Joh 19:38), yet now openly besought Pilate and took the body away. By laying the Lord in his own new tomb, this rich man fulfilled the prophecy that Messiah would make “his grave…with the rich in his death” (Isa 53:9). Arimathaea preaches the courage of a late-ripening faith. When the bold disciples had fled, the secret one came forward; when it was most perilous to be counted with Christ, Joseph confessed Him at the tomb. Grace makes the timid brave in the decisive hour, and the honour of burying the Lord fell not to the loud but to the faithful. The town’s name endures because one of its sons dared to love Christ openly when it cost the most.

corruption_summary: The home of Joseph who buried Jesus; the entry recovers the courage of a late-ripening faith that confessed Christ when it was most costly.
corruption_paragraphs: Arimathaea raises no modern controversy, but the deed of its son rebukes the cowardice of secret discipleship that never comes into the light. Joseph had been a disciple secretly, for fear of the Jews; yet in the hour when the bold had fled, grace made the timid man brave, and he confessed Christ openly at the tomb.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that saving faith, however late-ripening, at last confesses Christ before men, whatever the cost. Joseph fulfilled prophecy by laying the Lord with the rich in death, and won an honour the loud disciples missed. The Lord is patient with the fearful and secret believer, but He calls him out of hiding: whosoever is ashamed of Christ before men, of him will Christ be ashamed. Arimathaea assures the trembling disciple that the same grace which gave Joseph courage at the cross can make him also confess his Lord in the decisive hour.
